bearings.paper_claim: Communal styles (human narrative, affect, positive emotion) were higher among female MPs early in the period. Positive emotion and affect show no consistent significant gender gap by the latest years; the human narrative gap narrows gradually but is not stated to reach zero. For six of eight styles gender explains less between-MP style variation at the end of the period than at the start. For the converging styles the share of MP-level variation explained by gender falls 29 to 60 percent comparing pre-2007 with post-2007; the converging styles are not named individually. Window: UK Commons May 1997 to March 2019. Denominator: MP-by-session variation (R2-style metric).
bearings.paper_location: p.23-27 (results); p.9 Table 1; p.25 (29-60 range); p.26-27 (communal decline); p.4 (six of eight)
bearings.system_side: persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) - .40 z(agency) from LLM cue shares (agency_communion_llm.py), blended at PERSONA_W 0.30 for members with 15 or more classified sentences (receptivity_layer.py). No gender term in the persona code. Comments record cooperation_v2 gender -.021 and reactivity as gender-clean. The claimed party signature (communion D .099 vs R .049) was not found in fec/members or the audit files searched.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/receptivity_layer.py lines 139-158 and 191 (persona build and blend); fec/members/receptivity_layer.py lines 70 and 98 (gender-clean comments); fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py (cue codebook)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper gap is on UK floor speech using embedding-expanded dictionaries; the system uses Birkenmaier-Lechner LLM cue shares on US congressional sentences, a different instrument. Transfer holds only if US cue shares show a gender gap. Check: persona_susc_z against the legislators.csv gender column, partialled on party. Stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Formula, 0.30 weight, 15-sentence threshold and absence of any gender term confirmed in code. Paper wording overstated for human narrative (only positive emotion and affect have no consistent gap). The party .099/.049 figure was not located and stays unverified.

bearings.paper_claim: Negative emotion runs against the stereotype: women use more of it than men for much of 1997-2019. Gender explains about 2 percent of MP-level variation in negative emotion in 1997-2007 and about 9 percent after 2007. For negative emotion the divergence is almost entirely differential replacement of MPs, with a near-zero within-MP gender difference (supplement Fig S8). The main text says neither replacement nor within-MP change alone explains the convergence across styles. Window: UK Commons 1997-2019.
bearings.paper_location: p.23-25 and p.25 (R2 figures); p.28 (main-text mechanism statement); S30-S35 and Fig S8 (replacement decomposition)
bearings.system_side: affective_n is the sum of LLM affective facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility), residualized on E then on party and z-scored (emit_affective_n.py). The LIWC composite is kept only as a convergent anchor (r +.24 per code comment). The file has no gender term, so there is no gender residualization or gender audit. Input source (interview text) was not traced further.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/emit_affective_n.py lines 39-56 (facet sum, E and party residualization, z-score, LIWC anchor comment); no gender term in the file
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies only if US members negative-affect expression differs by gender in the interview genre. The paper measures negative emotion as a dictionary score on UK floor speech, not the LLM facets, so this is a different operationalisation. Any chamber-composition effect needs a stated window. The interview-genre transfer figures cited by the analyst were not rechecked.
bearings.verifier_note: The 2 and 9 percent figures and the replacement result hold for negative emotion. The paper does not say replacement explains divergence for all styles; the main text says neither mechanism alone explains convergence. The code description was confirmed. The components.txt staleness claim and the rho values were not checked.

bearings.paper_claim: Seed dictionaries expanded with GloVe word embeddings correlate with human coder judgements at 0.61 to 0.85 per style across the comparison and intensity tasks. Standard dictionaries do worse, e.g. positive emotion 0.38 and 0.34 against 0.70 and 0.71 for the embedding measure. Each coder completed about 70 comparisons per style on average. Six of eight styles use the embedding expansion, and the embedding measure beats standard dictionaries for every style except fact (bootstrap test).
bearings.paper_location: p.15-17 (method); Table S4 p.S17; p.S19 (comparison with standard dictionaries)
bearings.system_side: Closed-vocabulary posemo, negemo, anx and anger rates use published-exemplar word lists of about 20 to 32 words each (big5_traits.py), replaced by licensed LIWC .dic files if dropped into fec/liwc. Rates are z-scored and enter trait fits through weights. The paper validation covers UK debate sentences, not these lists.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/big5_traits.py lines 77-87 (CAT word lists) and 108-114 (dictionary hooks); word counts checked
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper validation is on UK House of Commons sentences with two coders. Using its embedding expansion on congressional text needs a fresh human-coded sample. Any change to trait inputs falls under change control and single-look discipline. This is not a finding that the current lists are wrong.
bearings.verifier_note: Correlation range, the 0.38 vs 0.70 positive-emotion comparison and the 70 comparisons per coder were re-read in the text. GloVe settings (150 dimensions, window 3) come from the extraction and were not separately re-read. Word-list sizes confirmed in code.
